title: What meditation research shows
hookLine: a 2014 review of 47 trials found moderate help for anxiety, depression and pain (Goyal et al., JAMA)

cards: Type does meditation work into a search bar and you get two kinds of answers. One camp says it changes everything: stress, sleep, focus, relationships, your whole brain.
The other rolls its eyes: it's sitting still, and the rest is marketing. Both sound confident. Neither usually says where the confidence comes from.
So instead of one study, or one enthusiast, let's see what holds when careful researchers gather up dozens of trials at once.

teach.h: GOYAL ET AL., JAMA INTERNAL MEDICINE, 2014.
teach.b: In 2014 a team led by Madhav Goyal at Johns Hopkins published a review in JAMA Internal Medicine. A review like this runs no new experiment; it collects the existing ones and weighs them together.

From thousands of published papers, they kept only randomized trials, where people were assigned by chance, and only those with an active comparison group, something like a health education class, so attention and hope were matched.
That's yesterday's question, compared to what, and it was the whole point. Forty-seven trials made the cut, with about thirty-five hundred people.
Mindfulness meditation programs, often around eight weeks long, showed moderate evidence of improving anxiety, depression and pain.
Moderate is a technical word here: it describes how confident the reviewers were, and the improvements themselves were small to moderate. For stress and quality of life, the evidence was low.
For attention, sleep, mood and weight, low or not enough to say.
And against other active treatments, like exercise, medication or therapy, there was no evidence meditation did better. So that's the honest shape. Not a miracle.
A real, modest help for some real problems, and no substitute for care when you need it. Some traditions on this path would say that isn't why they sit anyway. That's fair too.
But if someone asks whether the science says meditation helps, now you have a true answer. Moderate, and real.

how: Clinicians sometimes suggest mindfulness programs, often eight weeks long, alongside other care for anxiety, depression or chronic pain, drawing on reviews like Goyal et al.

games.q: you're reviewing meditation studies. which trials make the strongest evidence?
o: randomized trials with an active comparison group.
the ones with the biggest headlines.
games.why: Goyal's team kept only randomized trials against active controls, like a health education class.

practice: Before you sit, take a quick reading: on a scale of one to ten, how settled do you feel right now? Then sit with the breath, noticing and coming back, and when the bell rings, take the reading again.
There's no right answer, just one small, honest data point.

wordCard.voice: Goyal, whose 2014 review of 47 trials found moderate evidence that meditation programs ease anxiety, depression and pain.

carryVoice: Your line: moderate, and real. A modest help is still a help. Day three hundred five, done.
